title: Filling the Planning Gap
author: Foster, Pete
summary: Pete Foster argues that lesson-planning proformas often distort planning by implying lessons run on a fixed track, making it hard for teachers to genuinely adapt mid-lesson even when feedback tells them to. His fix is building specific planning habits rather than better templates: planning explicitly for thinking, using Doug Lemov's concept of ratio, how many students are thinking and how hard, rather than just for content coverage; planning to embed and check new content with specific, low-stakes checks like hands-down questions or mini-whiteboards; and planning to adapt, by treating certain lesson sections as "elastic" that can expand or contract based on what a check reveals. He works through a science example, teaching acceleration and catching the unfamiliar word "initial," to show how a planned check can surface exactly where understanding breaks down, and offers concrete adaptation moves, extending the "We Do" phase of a worked example, turning an independent task into a "completion problem" by starting it for students, and having backup questions ready for when a misconception surfaces. He closes with two general-purpose habits any teacher can have ready for unexpected moments: Turn and Talk, with a specific four-part routine of question, phrase, timeframe, and starting signal, and mini-whiteboards, both designed to buy processing time and generate a genuine understanding check without derailing the lesson.
points: Foster's core diagnosis is that planning proformas encourage a false sense that lessons are "on a track," making feedback like "you saw they didn't understand and you ploughed on" fair to give but nearly impossible for teachers to act on without deliberately built-in adaptation habits.

His acceleration/"initial" example shows a planned check catching a specific vocabulary gap invisible to content-focused planning, illustrating exactly why "plan to check" has to be separate from "plan for content."

His "turn an independent task into a completion problem" move, starting the task for students rather than expecting a fully independent attempt, offers a concrete middle step between full teacher control and full independence.
His four-part Turn and Talk routine, question, phrase, timeframe, starting point, is explicitly designed as a reusable habit for in-the-moment uncertainty, not a scripted activity planned in advance.
quotes: I know I have received, and have definitely given feedback like Don’t be afraid to adapt the lesson when I’m in the room. You saw they didn’t understand and you ploughed on. This feedback is unfair because it lacks specificity.
Doug Lemov’s idea of Ratio is useful here – how many students are thinking in any given task and how cognitively challenging is the thinking that they are doing.

You explain acceleration using a video and model a visual representation of acceleration on the board. You’re going to want to gradually model the process of calculating acceleration but first you check students have understood the terms and the process with a planned quiz of this knowledge.
When planning, it might be useful to see some tasks or sections of lessons as elastic, able to stretch to their need.

If that English teacher expects students to be able to write an analytical paragraph but the check has revealed uncertain understanding of the paragraph structure, they can start the task itself. Instead of expecting an independently written paragraph, the teacher can start it and get students to finish or start sections and expect students to complete.
